quote: Crushed, Everett left academic physics, invented the general use of Lagrange multipliers in optimization problems, and became a multimillionaire.
content: Lagrange multipliers were in general use in optimization for a century and a half before Everett; what Everett published in 1963 was the “generalized Lagrange multiplier method” for a class of discrete resource-allocation problems (Everett (1963)), a real contribution to operations research and not the invention of the technique. He did leave academic physics, for Pentagon weapons-systems analysis and then for Lambda Corporation, which he co-founded; his biographer records financial success, then the firm’s decline, chronic drinking, and death of a heart attack at fifty-one, with the family in some difficulty (Byrne, The Many Worlds of Hugh Everett III, 2010, a book with no DOI). “Multimillionaire” is not the word the biography uses. The sentence is a fable of the vindicated outsider, told in the shape the sequence needs, and the annotator notes it because the sequence’s argument about the sociology of physics rests on such fables.

quote: “Oh my! So you’re saying, Huve, that physicists detect superposition in microscopic systems, and work out quantitative equations that govern superposition in every single instance they can test. And for thirty years, not one person says, ‘Hey, I wonder if these laws happen to be universal.’ ”
content: Someone did, and the satire’s punchline is false about the two people it names. Von Neumann’s 1932 treatment applies the unitary laws to the measuring apparatus and to the observer’s body, follows the chain as far as one likes, and shows that it never terminates in a definite outcome; he then introduced the projection postulate explicitly as a second process, because the universal application he had just carried out did not reproduce what was observed. Schrödinger, in his 1952 Dublin lectures, said that the quantum theorist who takes the equation seriously must accept that it describes “simultaneous alternatives” that are all real, and called the idea one that would be regarded as lunacy, five years before Everett (Bitbol, Schrödinger’s Philosophy of Quantum Mechanics, 1996; Barrett, The Quantum Mechanics of Minds and Worlds, 1999). The idea of applying the laws universally was not unthought; it was thought, and set aside, because it leaves the Born statistics and the definiteness of experience unexplained, which is the problem this sequence’s last essay concedes is open. The alternate-Earth device also has a real counterpart the essay does not use: a realist theory did come first, de Broglie’s in 1927, and the field rejected it. Whether that rejection was contingent is the subject of Cushing’s book; the answer is not the one the satire assumes.

quote: “Huve, this is a world where every single physicist, and probably the whole damn human species, is too dumb to sign up for cryonics! We’re talking about the Earth where George W. Bush is President.”
content: The closing joke stacks three of the author’s commitments, many-worlds, cryonics and a political preference, and treats disagreement with any of them as evidence of a stupid world. Cryonics is the odd one out, since its scientific status is not comparable: no mammal has been revived from cryopreservation at the temperatures involved, the ice-damage and toxicity problems of vitrification at whole-organ scale remain unsolved (the best result, a rabbit kidney vitrified and transplanted with partial function, is Fahy et al., 2009, and it has not been extended), and the scientific community’s scepticism is a judgment about evidence, not a symptom. Book II’s annotations on the cryonics-versus-skydiving comparison made the same point. A reader may agree with all three commitments; the argument offered for the bundle is that people who lack them are dumb, which is the argument from the outgroup that the book’s essays on politics spend a sequence warning against.
